newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-AUSTRALIAN EYES WORLD CUP GLORY FROM SERIE A.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-AUSTRALIAN EYES WORLD CUP GLORY FROM SERIE A.

text.p: Australia are dreaming of international soccer glory, with a place in next year's World Cup finals as the target and former England coach Terry Venables helping their cause.
Such sporting ambition in a country more noted for cricket, rugby union and Australian Rules football fired Paul Okon's imagination.
It also gave him reason to believe he might become something of a sports celebrity back home in Australia when he signed a three-year contract with Italian serie A side Lazio this season.
As it is, the 24-year-old Lazio sweeper's rise from semi-professionalism to the serie A, still considered by many to be the world's top league, has got only scant mention in the Australian press.
"I've only done one interview with an Australian journalist in my seven months here," Okon told Reuters after a session at the Rome club's new training ground.
"It's not enough to help the game back home," he said, referring to the fact that his career at Lazio has not created the kind of enthusiasm generated by some other sports.

Okon, Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich and West Ham winger Stan Lazaridis head an ever-expanding list of Australian players who have been tempted overseas as full-time professionals, an option denied them at home because of the game's shaky finances.
"Football in Australia is played at 7.30 on a Saturday evening and people ask themselves: 'Am I going to watch semi-professionals run around?'" Okon said.
The contrast with soccer-mad Italy, where most players are household names, could not be more striking, he added.

"The Italian league has a lot of colour about it. The people live for the game," said Okon, who moved to Rome after being voted Belgian league player of the year at Club Brugge last season after five years at that club.
Before that, he had been semi-professional with the Australian club Marconi in Sydney.
"You have to go abroad to test yourself and become as good as possible," he said.
Ambitious Soccer Australia chairman David Hill, however, has made it his priority to stop the exodus of top players by raising the game's profile at home.
In a surprise signing last year, Venables agreed to help Australia's national side attempt to reach the 1998 World Cup finals in France.
"Everybody is excited (about Venables)," Okon said. "To get to the World Cup will attract money and sponsorship. It's our only chance to get the game up and running on a professional level."
The Australian league, which consists of 12 semi-professional teams, will only hold on to its top players if it turns fully professional, he added
"So long as you are semi-professional you don't have the mentality to do your best.
"If it's professional the quality of the game will improve, the spectators will come and you won't lose so many players abroad," Okon said.
But Hill believes there is another, more thorny problem restricting the success of Australian soccer.
Of the 12 league clubs, over half evolved from within particular ethnic communities of post-war immigrants.
The insularity and fervent nationalism of these clubs, Hill argues, is stopping the game appealing to a wider Australia.

Okon, who has an Italian mother and grew up playing with Bosnich for Marconi, a club backed by Sydney's Italian community, said he did not agree with official policy to eradicate the ethnic flavour of Australia's league.
"In Australia you don't support the team where you live, it's your nationality. It will always come down to nationality," he said.
Hill banned clubs this season from including European national flags in their logos which pushed one strident critic to accuse him of "ethnic cleansing".
"He believes that's what is holding the game back," Okon said. "But Marconi will always be Marconi. You can't change that."
